sections.html:
Bozeman lies in the Gallatin Valley of southwest Montana, 4,817 feet above sea level. Butte is 84 miles away to the west, Billings 125 miles to the east, and Yellowstone National Park 93 miles south. Interstate 90 passes through. The count in 2020 was 53,293 people, the 2025 estimate is 58,814, and the wider metro area holds about 118,960.

Bozeman Health and Montana State University head the employer list, with firms such as Simms Fishing Products and Mystery Ranch behind them and a growing group of technology and biotech companies. Jobs like these keep newcomers arriving, so a Bozeman house usually draws interest. The questions sellers ask tend to be about tax rates and paperwork rather than demand.

sections.h2: Snow, ice and an older house
sections.html:
Long, snowy winters and fairly warm summers shape Bozeman houses, and the air at 4,817 feet can cool sharply after sundown. Up to 24 inches of precipitation falls in a year. Inspectors tend to study how the roof handles snow load, whether ice builds at the eaves and how the exterior wood has held up.

Deferred repairs do not have to be finished before a sale. Cash buyers accept the house as is and price in the work that remains, while a buyer with a mortgage may come back with a repair list after inspection.

Gallatin County's treasurer takes Bozeman payments at 311 West Main, Room 103. Call 406-582-3030 or write treasurer@gallatin.mt.gov between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday to Friday. Value disputes and taxable value questions belong to the Department of Revenue's Bozeman office, 406-582-3400.

2026 real property, first halfDecember 7, 2026

Standard state scheduleNovember 30 and May 31, each at 5 p.m.
Late payment2% penalty plus 5/6 of 1% interest per month

If a lender or title company already pays on your behalf, confirm that before sending your own check.

For 2026 the state steps the rate up in tiers for a primary residence or long-term rental, opening at 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value. Vacation homes, short-term rentals and empty residential lots skip the tiers and pay 1.90% throughout; the Department of Revenue counts VRBO and Airbnb style rentals in that group. Owners of a second home or short-term rental near Bozeman should weigh that cost before choosing to hold or sell.

A buyer moving in can request the lower homestead rate, but it does not transfer with the deed. The new owner files for it.

The choices are an agent, doing it yourself, or taking cash. An agent exposes the house to the largest group of buyers, along with showings, a commission and renegotiation once the inspection is back. Doing it yourself saves the commission and makes you responsible for every form. A cash offer normally means as is, closing when you say.

Mechanics stay constant. Your signature on the deed is acknowledged by a notary, then the Gallatin County Clerk and Recorder receives it with a Realty Transfer Certificate. The recording charge is $20 for the first page and $10 for each added page. Any tax you still owe is a lien, cleared at closing.

Interested in cash for your Bozeman house? The form above takes the address. You get a written offer back, and declining costs nothing.

A lender-backed buyer brings an appraisal, underwriting and often a repair list. None of those apply to cash, which leaves the title work as the main thing setting your timeline. Get the offer in writing, pin down the closing date, and look at the settlement statement to see how recording costs and unpaid tax are treated.

Two things surprise Bozeman sellers. Rental and second-home status brings a higher rate than a primary residence, and the title company must split the first and second tax halves between you and the buyer. Bring both up early, ideally before you sign anything, so there are no numbers to argue about at closing.

• Locate your newest tax statement and any mortgage payoff figure.
  • Let the title company know who pays the county tax, you or a lender.
  • Make sure names match exactly on the deed and the Realty Transfer Certificate.
  • Sign the deed before a notary.
  • Check that the clerk and recorder gets the deed, certificate and fee.
  • Read the settlement statement before funds go out.
  • Keep a copy of the recorded deed and the final statement for your tax records.

Nothing here is hard, but each step depends on another person, so beginning a week early takes out most of the stress. Should a lien or unpaid tax surface, the title company takes it from your proceeds and closing carries on.

Have your address or parcel number, your latest statement and the name on the account in front of you. Then ask three things: which halves are already paid, whether December 7, 2026 applies to your parcel, and what the payoff would be on a specific closing date. A call before you accept an offer prevents a hiccup at the signing table. A question about why the value is what it is goes to the Department of Revenue's Bozeman office instead.

sections.h2: A rough timeline for a cash sale
sections.html: The first stage is the offer. You describe the house, we answer in writing, and you choose. Acceptance sends the file to a title company, which searches the record for liens and unpaid tax and drafts the documents. After the notary signing, the deed and certificate are recorded and money moves once the settlement statement is approved. With a mortgage buyer, an appraisal and lender review sit in the middle, and that is usually where schedules stretch.

Pay late and you owe a 2% penalty plus 5/6 of 1% interest each month, while the unpaid amount turns into a lien on the house. Selling is still an option. The treasurer's office gives you the balance, the title company receives it, and the amount comes out of your proceeds when you close. With cash there is no lender approval to hold things up. The treasurer answers payment questions, and the Department of Revenue's Bozeman office explains the value behind your bill.

Bozeman also has a Community Housing Program run by the city, which publishes housing data and help resources for people who live, work and study in town. It is worth a look if you are weighing a sale against staying.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Bozeman?
faqs.a: The Gallatin County Treasurer, at 311 West Main, Room 103. The Department of Revenue's Bozeman office handles questions about market and taxable value.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 property tax rate on a Bozeman primary residence?
faqs.a: A tiered rate: 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value, 0.90% from $378,001 to $756,000, 1.10% from $756,001 to $1,511,999 and 1.90% above that. Second homes and short-term rentals pay a flat 1.90%.

faqs.q: When is the 2026 first-half tax payment due in Bozeman?
faqs.a: December 7, 2026 for the first half of 2026 real property tax, as Gallatin County lists it. State default dates are November 30 and May 31, each at 5 p.m.
Almost all of Bozeman is in the Bozeman Elementary and Bozeman High School Districts. A small area is in the Belgrade districts.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Bozeman house as is?
faqs.a: Yes. The sale still needs a notarized deed, a Realty Transfer Certificate and recording with the county clerk and recorder.
